analysis.investment_thesis: Anupam Rasayan is a capital-hungry specialty chemicals business currently earning a 3.32% ROE while trading at 85x earnings — one of the worst combinations I can imagine. Revenue has declined two years running (₹1,602 Cr in 2023 to ₹1,437 Cr in 2025) while the company has burned through hundreds of crores in capex with no return to show for it.
key_strengths: Long-term contract-based revenue model with global agrochemical, pharma, and personal care players provides some revenue visibility
Diversified geography (Europe, Japan, North America, China) reduces single-market dependency
IPO-funded balance sheet (equity raised in 2021) means the leverage, while rising, hasn't yet become existential
key_risks: ROE of 3.32% is catastrophic — the business is destroying shareholder value at current capital costs while pricing implies it deserves a premium
Finance costs have grown from ₹24 Cr (2019) to ₹112 Cr (2025), a 29% CAGR, eating deeply into operating profits as debt rises
Revenue and profits have been declining for two consecutive years despite heavy capex — the expansion is not yet yielding returns
red_flags: P/E of 85x with ROE of 3.32% — this is pure speculation, not investing; you cannot justify this valuation with any rational cash flow model
Free cash flow was -₹440 Cr in 2025 and -₹644 Cr in 2024; the company has generated negative FCF in 4 of 6 years
CWIP surged to ₹609 Cr in 2024 before falling to ₹58 Cr in 2025 — massive ongoing capex cycle with uncertain returns and significant execution risk
analysis.detailed_analysis:
If I were to design the antithesis of an ideal Berkshire investment, Anupam Rasayan would be a strong contender. It is capital-intensive, it earns returns well below its cost of capital (3.32% ROE), it generates negative free cash flow most years, and it is priced as if it were a high-quality compounder. The specialty chemicals sector can produce excellent businesses — but only those with proprietary processes, pricing power, and high returns on capital. Anupam's returns suggest it has none of the above at scale.

The company's own financials tell the story: capex of ₹716 Cr in 2024 and ₹410 Cr in 2025 produced revenue growth of exactly zero — revenue declined in both years. Finance costs have quadrupled in six years. The market is apparently paying 85x earnings for the hope that future capacity additions will eventually generate adequate returns. I am not in the business of paying for hope. This stock earns a firm pass.
